content: Ebastine, marketed under various trade names such as Evastin, Kestine, Ebastel, Aleva, and Ebatrol, is classified as an H1 antihistamine. It is characterized by a low likelihood of causing drowsiness or sedation. The chemical structure of ebastine was first described in patents registered in Europe and the United States. Due to its poor water solubility, the compound is frequently provided in a micronized form to enhance its bioavailability. Ebastine is a second-generation H1 receptor antagonist primarily indicated for the treatment of allergic rhinitis and chronic idiopathic urticaria. It is available in 10 mg and 20 mg tablets, as well as in fast-dissolving tablet formulations and pediatric syrup. The recommended daily dosage is flexible, ranging from 10 mg to 20 mg, depending on the severity of the condition being treated. Ebastine is marketed globally under various brand names, including Ebet, Ebastel FLAS, Kestine, Kestine LIO, Kestine LYO, Estivan LYO, Evastel Z, and Ebatrol, among others. Following oral administration, ebastine undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism in the liver, mediated by the cytochrome P450 3A4 enzyme system. This metabolic process converts ebastine into its active carboxylic acid metabolite, carebastine. The conversion is nearly complete, ensuring the pharmacological activity of the drug. Clinical data derived from over 8,000 patients across more than 40 clinical trials and studies have demonstrated the efficacy of ebastine in managing intermittent allergic rhinitis, persistent allergic rhinitis, and other related conditions. Ebastine has been shown to have a favorable safety and tolerability profile. It does not cause cognitive or psychomotor impairment and exhibits no sedative effects beyond those observed with placebo. Additionally, it has demonstrated cardiac safety, with no evidence of QT interval prolongation. The incidence of commonly reported adverse events was comparable between ebastine and placebo groups, further supporting its safety profile. While animal studies in pregnant subjects have shown no risk to the fetus, there is a lack of corresponding data in humans. It is also unknown whether ebastine is excreted into breast milk.
